Saul. The first King of Israel, anointed by the prophet Samuel around 1050 BCE to lead Israel against Philistine invasion. Though initially successful and charismatic, his reign deteriorated as he grew jealous of the young warrior David, whom he persecuted relentlessly. His story illustrates the dangers of pride and disobedience: rejected by God, he died alongside his sons at the Battle of Mount Gilboa.

Saul was chosen by Samuel as Israel's first king around 1050 BCE after the people demanded a monarch to unify them against external military threats, particularly the iron-equipped Philistines who dominated the coastal plains and threatened Israelite autonomy. He came from a humble background, a man of the tribe of Benjamin initially searching for his father's lost donkeys when he encountered Samuel. Yet he possessed impressive physical stature, and from his shoulders upward was taller than any of the people, and demonstrated genuine military prowess and tactical acumen.

Saul achieved early military success, consolidating Israel's fragmented tribal territories into a unified kingdom, establishing a standing professional army distinct from militia levies, and initially pushing back Philistine encroachment and other regional enemies. However, he grew increasingly erratic and paranoid as his reign progressed, exhibiting mood swings and what many interpreters view as mental illness. Samuel announced God's rejection of Saul, stating the kingship would pass to another, which amplified his psychological deterioration.

Saul developed a consuming, irrationally intense jealousy of David after the young warrior's military victories against the Philistines, most famously his defeat of the giant Goliath in single combat. He pursued David relentlessly across the Judean wilderness for years, using his royal resources and army to hunt his rival, yet David repeatedly spared Saul's life when opportunities to kill him arose—a mercy that deepened Saul's shame and desperation.

Before his final battle, Saul consulted the witch of Endor via necromancy, seeking counsel from the dead prophet Samuel about his coming fate, a religiously transgressive act violating his own laws against sorcery and psychologically revealing his despair. He died at the Battle of Mount Gilboa around 1010 BCE when he and his sons, including his heir Jonathan, fell to Philistine forces. Rather than face capture and execution, he reportedly fell on his own sword, ending the house of Saul and paving the way for David's rise to power.
